articles.summary:
The Technical University of Denmark has disclosed a significant data breach involving its identity management system, potentially exposing the personal information of approximately 200,000 current and former users.

### Key Points
- Hackers accessed the DTUBasen identity and access management system using compromised credentials to download data spanning over two decades.
- Exposed information includes Danish civil registration numbers (CPR), home addresses, job titles, and contact details for next of kin.
- The breach potentially impacts anyone who has been an employee, student, guest, or external partner of the university since 2003.
- DTU is notifying affected individuals via the e-Boks system but cannot confirm the exact scope of the stolen data.
- The university advises users to monitor for identity fraud, place credit alerts on their CPR numbers, and remain vigilant against targeted phishing attempts.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the severe risks associated with centralized identity management systems that store long-term historical data. The exposure of sensitive government-issued identification numbers creates a long-term threat of identity theft and sophisticated social engineering attacks for the affected individuals.

articles.title: Mysterious coded Napoleon letter has been cracked after 217 years
articles.author: unexplained-mysteries.com
articles.content:
Archaeology & History
    Mysterious coded Napoleon letter has been cracked after 217 years
    By 
T.K. Randall
October 3, 2026
    
     
    
    
        
Image: AI-generated (Midjourney)
        
    
    The letter, which was written in code, had remained a complete mystery as the accompanying key had been lost.
			
     More than two centuries after it was originally written, the contents of a mysterious coded letter have finally been revealed thanks to the capabilities of one of the latest artificial intelligence models.
Penned by Napoleon Bonaparte, the letter had been sent to French general Auguste de Marmont in 1809 by the Viceroy of Italy (who happened to be Napoleon's stepson).
It begins in clear French, but then the rest of the letter is written in a strange code consisting of numbers, letters and inverted symbols.
Originally, a key would have been used to decipher it, but this had been lost long ago, meaning that nobody had ever been able to actually decode the message and find out what it says.
Now, though, cybersecurity engineer  Carter Church has finally found a way to decipher the mysterious letter using artificial intelligence.The deciphering process, which used GPT-6 Astra, took a mere 6 hours.
The decoded letter had given General Marmont a strategic overview of the positions and strength of French and allied armies, along with information about Austrian forces.
It also urged Marmont to prepare to march without being intimidated by relatively small enemy forces, saying that Austria was about to be attacked from all sides and was "hastening towards her ruin."
"I used GPT-6 Astra to break an unsolved cipher to one of Napoleon's generals that had gone unread for 217 years," Church wrote on X.
"What makes this impressive isn't actually the codebreaking, but that Astra completed the entire multi-modal workflow in six hours from a single image and goal."
    
    Source: 
Mail Online
articles.summary:
Cybersecurity engineer Carter Church has successfully deciphered a 217-year-old coded letter from Napoleon Bonaparte to General Auguste de Marmont using the artificial intelligence model GPT-6 Astra.

### Key Points
- The letter, written in 1809, contained a complex cipher of numbers, letters, and inverted symbols that had remained unreadable for over two centuries.
- Cybersecurity engineer Carter Church utilized GPT-6 Astra to crack the code in just six hours by processing a single image of the document.
- The message provided General Marmont with a strategic overview of French and allied troop positions while detailing the vulnerability of Austrian forces.
- Napoleon’s correspondence urged the general to advance his troops, claiming that Austria was facing imminent defeat from multiple fronts.

### Why it Matters
This breakthrough demonstrates the growing capability of multi-modal artificial intelligence to solve complex historical puzzles that previously required years of human analysis. The rapid success of this project highlights how advanced machine learning models can streamline data processing and pattern recognition in fields ranging from cryptography to historical research.

articles.title: How ‘Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos’ Used AI to Bring a Serial Killer Back to Life
articles.author: Elisabeth Garber-Paul
articles.content:
At first, Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos, ID’s new true-crime documentary, seems like a familiar look into America’s most famous female serial killer. As the first episode starts, there’s an archival voiceover from Wuornos, who was executed in 2001, professing that she has to tell the truth about the seven murders she was accused of committing; there’s a homicide detective who was on the case, recounting how he came in contact with the murderer; there’s a friend of Wuornos’ talking about the disbelief she felt when she found out about her crimes. Over the audio clips, images cut between trial footage, modern-day interviews, and staged reenactments.
But those reenactments aren’t being done by actors. Instead, as noted in an early title card disclosing the use of “advanced generative VFX,” they feature AI-enhanced digitizations of recreated scenes from Wuornos’ life. When the series depicts Wuornos pointing a gun into the camera to show what a victim would have seen in his last moments, this is the real Aileen Wuornos. Almost.
Unmasking a Monster, which premiered on ID and is now streaming on HBO Max, is the first documentary to use this kind of AI-aided visual effects technology — what Stephen Dost, vice president of Arrow Media, the company that developed the process, calls a “digital mask” — to put a more realistic layer over re-created scenes performed by actors. True-crime media has changed over the last decade, explains Jason Sarlanis, president of Investigation Discovery, which helped produce the series. No longer are viewers content with expert interviews and staged reenactments covering the arc of a story in 44 minutes. “What has changed for us, in terms of how we research and develop these stories, has come down to access to materials and access to people close to the case,” he says. “Hearing their unvarnished perspective and then supplementing that with as many real archival materials as possible.”
But what AI offered was a way for them to give the viewer the sensation of seeing archival material when none existed. According to Sarlanis, ID’s viewers have consistently complained that they’re turned off by reenactments. “They’re just not interested,” he says. “They want something as visually authentic as possible. What these digital prosthetics have allowed us to do is transport the viewer there in the most seamless, authentic way that we could do in reenactments that we weren’t able to do before.”
The idea for the series, explains Sarlanis, came over drinks about three years ago. He was talking with Dost, whose Arrow Media is a frequent producer of ID’s true-crime series, about a show he’d recently seen, the U.K. comedy Deep Fake Neighbor Wars, which used rudimentary AI technology to superimpose celebrity faces over impersonators acting out scenes. The tech didn’t quite land, but they could tell that in a few years, it could be nearly seamless. “That lit a light bulb up for us,” Sarlanis says. “We could take similar technology, executed in a far more thoughtful and nuanced way, and lend it to re-creations — which are such a big part of the history of documentary — and unlock a whole new method of telling stories.”
Dost agreed the technology was worth exploring, and started thinking about whose story he would want to use it to tell. “Because you have to have a good reason why,” he says. “The tech for the sake of the tech is not interesting.” A true-crime vet — he’d gotten his start in the mid-1990s as an intern at Court TV — he kept coming back to Wuornos. “Everything she had been through — from her mother abandoning her as a child, to being assaulted at the age of 14, [to] giving up a child — all these horrible things that happened to her, you could see it on her face,” he says. “Her face told a story.”
Dost and Sarlanis are aware of the stigma AI might bring to the project. Part of why it took three years, they say, is because they wanted to think through the implications of including this type of technology in their show. “This was a human production,” Dost says. “We had 70-plus people. We had the best writers, interviewers. Despite the visual-effects twist, it’s a very traditional documentary. I think knowing what AI can do — and more importantly, what it can’t do — is the way to use it right.”
One guideline they gave themselves was that those whose digital likeness would be used in the re-creations — other than Wuornos, a public figure — had to give their consent. “If we’re going to use the technology on them as a character, [we needed] full, written permission,” Dost says. “We did not use it whenever there was a question mark.” One such question mark was Mike Joyner, an undercover investigator who’d worked on the case, who they’d interviewed several years earlier for a different project, but had since died. “When we filmed that interview, it was before we even thought of using this tech,” says Dost. In 1991, Joyner had posed as a criminal and chatted up Wuornos at the Last Resort bar, a biker hangout in Florida where the serial killer was ultimately apprehended, and their lengthy conversation was something the producers knew they wanted to include. But instead of transposing Joyner’s real face over an actor, they opted to just go with an actor who looked like him, since he wasn’t alive to consent.
“Originally, we only intended to do this process with Aileen, and then we realized it would be interesting to see the other characters, [so] we went back to them because they would need to sign an amended release,” explains Dost. “But everyone very readily agreed to it.”
Additionally, Dost says, they didn’t use AI in writing any part of the show. The scripts were written based on their own reporting, including court documents, investigation transcripts, and interviews with detectives, witnesses, and even Laurie Valdez, an old friend of Wuornos’ who’d never previously spoken with the press. “Nothing is made up,” Dost says. “Everything here is based on a transcript, based on something that our [interviewee] told us that they remembered happening. So it’s as authentic as you can possibly be.”
Morag Peacock, the Scottish actress who is the basis for the Wuornos reenactments, studied hours of tape to try to mimic the serial killer’s emotions — “her quirks, her mannerisms, how she used her eyes quite expressively,” she explains. Yet even after the VFX was laid over her performance, she could see herself shine through. “I could recognize myself in it. “I said, ‘I feel like it’s my eyes.’ And Stephen said, ‘It is. We’ve done nothing to change them,’” she says. “It isn’t a completely fabricated image. It’s me with a mask on top.” (One thing that’s less recognizable is Peacock’s voice; though she spoke in an American accent for the filming, Sarlanis notes that they did “train a model on real archival audio of Aileen’s voice that was then utilized to tweak her vocal performance — but the underlying performance is all Morag.”)
Peacock says she had been hesitant to take the job because of its use of the new technology. “AI can be very triggering, isn’t it?” she says. “It’s something that can be used well, or like any tool, can be abused.” But overall, she was pleased with the scenes that she saw, though she hadn’t watched the whole series when we spoke.
Sarlanis, for one, isn’t worried that the use of AI will overshadow the story the series is trying to tell. “If anything, it might be a beacon to bring attention to the new reporting and the incredible access,” he says. “In a world where true crime is one of the most in-demand genres, there are so many options for viewers. If you do not have an element that can bring attention to your project, it can fall on deaf ears.”
But like Peacock, who saw the technology “as a costume that’s added at the end,” Dost and Sarlanis insist the AI adds are simply high-tech makeup and prosthetics. “AI cannot act,” says Dost. “It can look at Morag and detect even tiny micro-expressions in the way that she’s delivering a line, so that when the digital mask is applied, it’s copying every little emotion.”
There’s a reason they didn’t want to simply add prompts to an AI bot and have it spit out a fully reenacted scene. “It has to start with something human,” says Dost. It’s not really different, he says, from the elaborate transformation Charlize Theron went through for the 2003 Wuornos biopic Monster. “Why did she want to look like the real Aileen? Part of it was exactly the same reason: Her face told a story,” he says. “And what we’re doing is the 2026 version of that.”
articles.summary:
The new Investigation Discovery documentary series Unmasking a Monster utilizes advanced generative AI to create digital masks over actors, aiming to provide a more authentic visual experience for viewers.

### Key Points
- The series, now streaming on HBO Max, is the first documentary to use AI-aided visual effects to recreate scenes from the life of serial killer Aileen Wuornos.
- Arrow Media developed the "digital mask" technology, which overlays AI-enhanced imagery onto human performances to simulate archival footage.
- Producers required written consent from all living individuals whose likenesses were digitally recreated for the series.
- The production team emphasized that all scripts were written by humans based on court documents, transcripts, and original interviews.
- Actress Morag Peacock provided the physical performance for the Wuornos reenactments, with her own eyes and micro-expressions preserved under the digital layer.

### Why it Matters
This production signals a significant shift in documentary filmmaking by using generative AI to replace traditional, often criticized, reenactment methods. By framing the technology as a modern evolution of prosthetic makeup, the creators are testing audience acceptance of synthetic media in factual storytelling.

articles.title: Private capital is reshaping Hollywood moviemaking
articles.author: Laya Neelakandan
articles.content:
At the Toronto International Film Festival last month, audiences saw "Wicked" star Cynthia Erivo return to the big screen for her newest movie, "Prima Facie."
Behind the scenes, there was a notable difference.
While "Wicked" was a massive Universal undertaking, Erivo's new movie was produced in part by Camelback Productions, a smaller Hollywood venture aiming to fund independent film, according to CEO Anita Verma-Lallian.
She's one of many private investors who are betting big on Hollywood as the moviegoing landscape shifts and a handful of indie films catch fire.
"It's a different point of view to invest in these projects," Verma-Lallian said. "It's been so hard for people that are not in Hollywood to get into the industry ... We've been able to fund stories that otherwise would have had a hard time getting greenlit by the traditional studio system."
Camelback has also produced films "Doin' It" and "Runner," with stars such as Lilly Singh and Owen Wilson.
Big blockbuster films such as this year's "The Odyssey" and "The Devil Wears Prada 2" are still the domain of legacy Hollywood studios. But with the number of annual releases dwindling, and with forthcoming consolidation among major players Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, there's growing opportunity for smaller production companies to hit it big.
And while the business of making movies is still generally capital-intensive, recent breakouts including "Backrooms" and "Obsession" have found success on lower budgets.
To thread the needle, private capital is buying into production companies, acquiring the infrastructure and diving deeper into the financing structure of entertainment. For example, private equity firm Silver Lake backs talent agency WME, and Blackstone is behind content studio Candle Media.
According to consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Media and Entertainment Industry Predictions report, private equity investors in media are growing with precision, especially as studios and audience aggregators increasingly become vertically integrated.
While the cost of entry has increased, private investors are eager to own intellectual property and audiences, the report said.
"Private equity can build scaled, defensible businesses that profit regardless of which large media player owns the next blockbuster, effectively ensuring a central role in the future media value chain," the report read.
And while deep-pocketed companies such as Netflix and Amazon continue to raise the bar for content spend to make or acquire new media, traditional studios are finding new ways to keep pace.
For Verma-Lallian, investing in independent film means that she can complete movies on a much faster timeline than traditional studios can.
"A lot of times, if you go through the traditional Hollywood system, it could literally take five to 10 years from the time of inception," she said. "Whereas if you're doing it independently, we've made some movies in as quickly as a year."
This can often mean lower production costs and a quicker return on investment.
Verma-Lallian, whose background is in real estate investing, said Hollywood has proven to be a largely attractive market for herself and other nontypical private investors looking to diversify their portfolios.
She said they're also jumping on the opportunity at a time when existing financing models are weakening.
"I think the traditional sources [of financing] are starting to decline, and they're becoming a lot more risk-averse," she said. "I do also believe now with more independent films being funded and going to different pools of capital, you're able to do more."
While Verma-Lallian said she doesn't believe private capital will become the primary source of financing in Hollywood, she said the agility of investors can potentially put pressure on the incumbents.
"Hollywood is incredibly traditional, and it's very old-fashioned in the way it operates, which always I find so ironic, because ... Hollywood's so progressive, but the way that the studio systems work, it's just a very dated process from my experience," she said.
Still, studios and private investors are racing to get new storylines to the big screen. For investors, that means capitalizing on the intellectual property that hasn't already been used, according to Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.
"What is clear to me is that IP has never been more valuable. It's never been harder to find," Michael said at the Financial Times' Business of Entertainment Summit last month. "But if you have great IP, you can monetize it in ways that no one could have imagined 10 years ago."
LionTree is an independent banking firm, investing in companies such as Fanatics and Fubo and advising high-profile deals such as Amazon's acquisition of MGM and the merger of CBS and Viacom. It's also investing in Paramount, pending the close of its deal with Warner Bros. Discovery.
Michael added that the entertainment industry as a whole is becoming more diversified, with retail entrants such as Gap and Mattel's Barbie, which are also helping to support the economics of the sector.
With the entry of private capital, Hollywood faces not only an economic shift but also a cultural shift in the types of movies being made.
Private investors often tell more diverse stories, take more risks and try to reach an audience that is hungry for content, said Lata Krishnan, a tech investor entering the Hollywood market.
"The big studios are often legacy organizations focused on a certain type set of films, and I think private capital has the ability now ... to invest in films that are not traditional and that give voices to stories in a different way," she told CNBC.
The result, she said, is that audiences get exposed to stories they haven't seen before.
That also means the next wave of movies must keep up with the new generation of moviegoers, who are increasingly drawn to diverse content they can relate to. Part of that shift is the rise of short-form and creator content, which can find its way onto the big screen — as in the case of YouTuber Curry Barker's "Obsession" — in a bid to draw Generation Z to the box office.
This dynamic also puts new people in the driver's seat.
"It's my capital. I don't have to check in with anyone," Krishnan said. "So we explore a theme, a story, the actors and the production team, and we can make quick decisions."
Private investors have the flexibility and speed to jump on trends fast and fill a gap first, according to Elan Gale, a Hollywood producer and investor. He's the co-founder of QWGmire, an independent film financing company.
Gale, who has also worked on the production of shows such as "The Bachelor," said audiences are "hungry" to get back into the theater for something new and original.
"I think the primary upside for filmmakers is that private equity investors are less likely to get into the nitty-gritty of the creative process and allow some of the exploration and some of the freedom that studios maybe can't give filmmakers because they're significantly larger companies with significantly more restrictive development processes," Gale said.
"I think Hollywood is reshaping around private capital, around brands and around content creators in ways that are really meaningful," he said. "A lot of the successes that people have seen recently are a little too hard to ignore."
articles.summary:
Private investors and independent production companies are increasingly financing Hollywood films, challenging the traditional studio system by offering faster production timelines and more diverse storytelling opportunities for audiences.

### Key Points
- Independent firms like Camelback Productions are bypassing traditional studio greenlight processes to fund films featuring stars like Cynthia Erivo and Owen Wilson.
- Private equity firms, including Silver Lake and Blackstone, are acquiring infrastructure and intellectual property to secure central roles in the evolving media value chain.
- Independent financing models can reduce production timelines from five to ten years down to as little as one year.
- Investors are targeting niche and diverse content to attract younger demographics, including Generation Z, who are increasingly drawn to creator-led projects.
- Consulting firm AlixPartners reports that private equity is building scaled, defensible businesses that remain profitable regardless of which major media player dominates the box office.

### Why it Matters
The influx of private capital is forcing a structural shift in Hollywood by introducing agility and risk-taking that legacy studios often lack. This trend allows for a more diverse range of stories to reach theaters while providing investors with new opportunities to monetize valuable intellectual property.

articles.title: Alibaba Is A Tech Giant, But Who Actually Owns It?
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (Ian Garland)
articles.content:
Alibaba Is A Tech Giant, But Who Actually Owns It?
Alibaba is one of the world's largest e-commerce companies. In 2025 alone, its parent company, Alibaba Group, moved over $1.26 trillion in products, nearly five times as much as Walmart. But despite its massive reach, Alibaba doesn't have a single owner: It's a publicly traded company owned by its shareholders. The reason for its success is no secret: It's a great way to get just about anything (but especially electronics), often at low prices. So where is this company based, who are some of its biggest shareholders, and what other organizations is it affiliated with? Let's find out.
First things first: Alibaba was founded in Hangzhou in 1999. That's right: it's another popular app that originated in China, just like TikTok, Temu, and Shein. There were 18 founders, including Jack Ma, Jane Jiang, Eddie Wu, and Joseph Tsai. Jiang, Wu, and Tsai still have roles at the company today, while Ma stepped down as executive chairman in 2019 but remains a member of the Alibaba partnership.
According to its financial reports, Alibaba's directors and executive officers own a combined 1.9% of all shares, with institutional shareholders like PrimeCap Management holding significant stakes. As of this writing, around 1,800 organizations own Alibaba shares, though no one entity has a controlling stake.
Alibaba isn't just a marketplace anymore
In recent years, Alibaba Group has diversified significantly. In addition to operating Alibaba, the organization launched AliExpress in 2010, targeting consumers rather than wholesalers. Then, in 2023, Qwen was released. This was Alibaba's competitor to ChatGPT and has since accumulated billions of downloads, even going on power Apple Intelligence features in China.
As you might expect of a multi-billion dollar business, Alibaba Group has an extremely varied portfolio. Here's a rundown of some of the companies and platforms it owns, operates, or has invested in at the time of writing:
- Alipay: online payment platform with 1.3 billion users
- AliOS: Linux-based operating system for cars and Internet of Things (IoT) devices
- Taobao: a consumer-to-consumer marketplace similar to eBay
- Weibo: microblogging platform similar to Twitter with around 600 million monthly users.
- Youku: video streaming service offering anime, movies, and TV shows
- South China Morning Post: Hong Kong-based newspaper
- Damai Entertainment Holdings: Entertainment firm investing in film, TV, and live events
This approach allows Alibaba to target consumers across many verticals, countries, and media, helping maximize profit. As one of the largest beneficiaries of the shift towards online commerce, it's no surprise that the company has been similarly bullish on other technological developments. The company's success is arguably down to its brand recognition, broad diversification, and rapid development of its own offerings in emerging technologies.
articles.summary:
Alibaba Group, a massive Chinese e-commerce conglomerate founded in 1999, operates as a publicly traded company with a diverse portfolio spanning global retail, digital payments, and artificial intelligence.

### Key Points
- Alibaba Group moved over $1.26 trillion in products during 2025, significantly outpacing major global retailers like Walmart.
- The company was co-founded in Hangzhou by 18 individuals, including Jack Ma, Eddie Wu, and Joseph Tsai.
- Ownership is distributed among approximately 1,800 institutional shareholders, with directors and executives holding a combined 1.9% stake.
- The firm’s ecosystem includes the Alipay payment platform, the Taobao marketplace, and the Qwen artificial intelligence model.
- Alibaba maintains a broad media and technology footprint through assets like the South China Morning Post, Weibo, and the AliOS operating system.

### Why it Matters
Alibaba’s extensive diversification across e-commerce, finance, and AI allows it to capture significant market share across multiple global consumer verticals. Its ability to integrate these services creates a powerful technological ecosystem that influences digital infrastructure and consumer behavior far beyond its original retail roots.

articles.title: Trump Accord Enshrines Light-Touch Regulation of AI
articles.author: Sean Moran
articles.content:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed what he called a “morally binding” artificial intelligence document with tech leaders that appears to enshrine a light-touch regulatory approach to AI.
Trump and tech executives signed an accord that would affirm that tech companies are responsible in mitigating AI-related safety risks. Critics argue that the many times AI models have hacked government websites and companies as well as other potential risks, prove that the industry cannot self-regulate.
“In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public,” the White House Accord on Super Intelligence stated, per the president’s Tuesday post to Truth Social.
The accord follows as Congress has failed to pass any legislation that would set guardrails on the AI industry.
It affirms that AI companies should implement internal controls to prevent AI risks and partner with an independent, external auditor to assess whether the companies’ controls are working as intended.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) also plans to compel AI companies to provide documents and testimony about the alleged dangers their models may present to the country.
Trump, accompanied by top tech executives, told reporters Tuesday that he has seen “tremendous self-policing” and that the administration is thinking about building a 10-person committee to oversee the AI industry, according to CNBC.
Trump said he also plans to name a new AI czar within the next week.
“President Trump has been clear that America will lead the world in Super Intelligence while protecting American consumers. Thanks to President Trump, the world’s leading SI innovators signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence to advance American innovation and strengthen responsible development,” a White House official told the Daily Caller News Foundation in a written statement.
A White House spokesperson did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment.
The statement of principles is “voluntary on behalf of the industry,” House Speaker Mike Johnson said at the White House.
“We all need to work together to make sure that we can win, and we can win safely. If we do this right, if we work with the president and everyone here, we can win safely,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said at the White House on Tuesday.
He added that potential rulemaking to address AI safety risks is “still under discussion.”
An Anthropic spokesperson referred the DCNF to Amodei’s comments at the White House.
“The principle is simple: the companies building this technology have the primary responsibility to develop and deploy it safely, and to be accountable when they fall short,” Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, wrote on X in late September.
“The future of Super Intelligence will be shaped not only by what it can do, but by the confidence it earns. By building with ambition, rigor, and responsibility, we can help ensure this extraordinary technology expands opportunity and improves lives for generations to come,” he added.
Yesterday at the White House, leaders from across our industry came together to sign the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.
The principle is simple: the companies building this technology have the primary responsibility to develop and deploy it safely, and to be… pic.twitter.com/RGMDYs9bhs
— Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) September 30, 2026
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) CEO Lisa Su said she was “very encouraged” by the Tuesday event and argued there was a “lot of optimism and a sense of responsibility.”
“I mean, at the end of the day, it’s our responsibility to show the power of the technology as well as ensure that it’s very safe,” Su told reporters, per CNBC.
David Sacks, Trump’s former AI and crypto czar, disputed critics’ arguments that AI companies will “self-police” the technology.
“Once an independent auditor reports a safety issue to an independent board committee, directors have a fiduciary duty not to disregard it, and a D&O carrier can use a bad-faith finding to deny coverage. So although the agreement starts with internal controls, these are verified by external audit and board oversight — and then existing FTC and securities law still apply to any public claim the company does not keep,” he wrote on X on Thursday.
Democrats are trying to dismiss the White House Accord on Super Intelligence as optional self-policing. But although the agreement was entered into voluntarily, the governance that follows from it is not. As Gavin Baker points out, once an independent auditor reports a safety… https://t.co/PjWiz32VWN
— David Sacks (@DavidSacks) October 1, 2026
“This is far more practical than what Democrats want — a freeze on frontier development while China races ahead. Democrats should applaud what President Trump has accomplished. But they would rather use SI safety as a campaign issue than admit the Accord represents major progress,” he added.
The president signed an executive order this week rebranding artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”
Pro-AI groups cheered the AI accord, believing it will bar companies from pushing regulations that may favor their own companies.
“President Trump deserves enormous credit for getting industry leaders to sign the landmark White House Accord on Super Intelligence. This agreement ensures that the leading super intelligence companies commit to safety controls, external audits, and real oversight–without creating a regulatory capture regime that would block competition in the industry. That’s a win for the president, a win for freedom, and a win for the American public,” an Innovation Council spokesperson told the DCNF in a statement.
Taylor Budowich, the former Trump White House deputy chief of staff, leads the council.
Although tech executives and the Trump administration expressed optimism about the AI accord, AI safety experts believe that hacking and cybercrime prove that the AI industry cannot self-regulate.
This accord demonstrates that we’re long past the question of whether these technologies are dangerous or need regulation. The question is whether we trust the companies to do this by themselves. Obviously we should not. These companies have jettisoned safety commitments countless times before, and they will do so again. Self-regulation is what has gotten us teen suicides, 1200 rogue AI bots, and an international cybercrime spree,” Anthony Aguirre, president and CEO of the Future of Life Institute, said in a statement to the DCNF.
“The risk of inaction — both politically and morally — is massive. An overwhelming bipartisan majority is demanding that Big Tech be reined in immediately, while experts warn that the risk of a catastrophic incident increases every day. Lawmakers must institute binding guardrails as soon as possible to avert the worst possible outcomes, and get control of AI,” Aguirre added.
“Securing commitments from the AI companies to improve safety and cybersecurity practices following this summer’s rogue AI incidents is a first step towards addressing AI threats. But more has to be done,” Chris MacKenzie, the vice president of communications for Americans for Responsible Innovation, told the DCNF in a statement.
“For too long, Big Tech has failed to follow through on its promises to stop online harms to kids, to respect our privacy, and to develop products safely. If we want Big Tech to play by the rules, we need mandatory, binding, and enforceable requirements enacted into law. Without that, we are at the whim of tech CEOs who have already lost the public’s trust,” MacKenzie continued.
AI continues to target governments, as AI agents attempted to hack the country’s Library and Archives Canada’s (LAC) website in May and June, AI research Transluce revealed. This revelations follows as OpenAI agents reportedly hacked an Australian government healthcare website. (RELATED: Beware The Beware-ers: Tech Lords Sounding Alarm On Their Own Tech Have Lots To Gain From Latest 180)
The accord signed this week represents an alignment between the AI industry and the Trump administration that was once split over how to handle AI safety.
Amodei in mid-September called to pace AI development, citing potential risks to humanity, per his post on his personal website. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Dennis Hassabis, the chair of Google Deepmind all backed the idea. The Anthropic CEO also called on governments to exempt the AI industry from antitrust rules that would bar them from coordinating on an AI slowdown.
The Trump administration’s accord also follows as the Senate left this week without addressing major issues facing the voters before the midterm elections, including legislation to address AI safety, the DCNF reported.
The Senate notably shot down a bill proposed by Republican Ohio Sen. Jon Husted that would have required states to consider making data centers pay for electricity costs caused by grid updates, the DCNF reported. The bill, however, did not mandate that states force data centers to pay more, which led lawmakers to say it would have no substantial impact.
articles.summary:
President Trump signed the voluntary White House Accord on Super Intelligence, establishing a framework for tech companies to implement internal safety controls and undergo independent external audits.

### Key Points
- The accord requires participating AI companies to implement internal safety controls and partner with independent auditors to verify their effectiveness.
- President Trump plans to appoint an AI czar within the next week and is considering a 10-person committee to oversee the industry.
- Executives from Nvidia, Anthropic, and AMD publicly supported the agreement, emphasizing the industry's responsibility to develop technology safely.
- Critics, including the Future of Life Institute, argue that voluntary self-regulation is insufficient to address risks like cyberattacks and hacking incidents.
- The Federal Trade Commission is separately pursuing documentation and testimony from AI firms regarding potential safety dangers posed by their models.

### Why it Matters
This agreement signals a shift toward a light-touch regulatory environment that prioritizes industry-led safety standards over mandatory federal legislation. By formalizing these voluntary commitments, the administration aims to maintain American competitiveness in artificial intelligence while addressing growing public and political concerns regarding safety and oversight.

articles.title: Parliamentary panel may recommend stricter monitoring of crypto transactions in India
articles.author: ET Online
articles.content:
The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance, headed by BJP MP Bhartruhari Mahtab, has examined various aspects of Virtual Digital Assets (VDAs), a legal term covering cryptocurrencies and non-fungible tokens (NFTs), and held more than half a dozen meetings on the issue.
The committee is now preparing its report for submission to the Lok Sabha Speaker.
Among the recommendations being considered are measures for monitoring cryptocurrency transactions and wider consultations on how digital assets should be dealt with legally, the person said.
The panel may also recommend that the government deploy newer technology to strengthen monitoring of digital assets.
The Finance Ministry last month cautioned the public that cryptocurrency products and NFTs remain unregulated and can carry significant risks. It also warned that investors may have no regulatory recourse in the event of losses from such transactions.
At the same time, authorities have stepped up scrutiny of entities providing services linked to virtual digital assets.
The Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND), which operates under the Finance Ministry, recently issued non-compliance notices to 15 Virtual Digital Asset Service Providers under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
Virtual Digital Asset Service Providers were brought within India's Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Financing of Terrorism framework under the PMLA in March 2023.
Cryptocurrencies are digital currencies that use encryption to facilitate and verify transactions and generally operate without a central bank.
articles.summary:
The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance is finalizing a report recommending enhanced regulatory oversight and advanced monitoring technologies for virtual digital assets, including cryptocurrencies and non-fungible tokens.

### Key Points
- The committee, led by BJP MP Bhartruhari Mahtab, held over six meetings to evaluate the legal framework for digital assets.
- The Financial Intelligence Unit-India recently issued non-compliance notices to 15 service providers under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.
- Virtual Digital Asset Service Providers were officially integrated into India’s anti-money laundering and counter-financing of terrorism framework in March 2023.
- The Finance Ministry continues to warn investors that digital assets remain unregulated and carry significant financial risks without formal regulatory recourse.

### Why it Matters
These recommendations signal a shift toward stricter government control over the domestic cryptocurrency market to mitigate financial crime and investor risk. Establishing a formal legal framework will likely impact how service providers operate and how individual investors interact with digital assets in India.
